analysis.one_liner: Bans stock trading by members of Congress, the President, Supreme Court Justices, and top Federal Reserve officials, and forces their finances into searchable public databases.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have banned stock trading by members of Congress, the President, Supreme Court Justices, and top Federal Reserve officials, was introduced with 3 cosponsors, referred to three House committees, and never received a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would ban members of Congress, the President and Vice President, Supreme Court Justices, and top Federal Reserve officials from trading individual stocks, commodities, futures, and cryptocurrency — they could hold only diversified funds like mutual funds or Treasuries, and would have to sell off or blind-trust conflicting holdings when they take office. It would also force any loans, contracts, or grants the federal government gives to these officials or their families to be disclosed, add a $500 fine for missing trade-disclosure deadlines, extend the rules to federal judges and Fed bank leaders, and require all of their financial filings to be posted online in searchable, downloadable databases. It never got a hearing or a vote in any committee and died when the 117th Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary citizens gain a rule that lawmakers, presidents, judges, and Fed officials cannot personally trade the stocks and cryptocurrencies their own decisions move, and can see those officials' federal loans, contracts, and grants in a searchable public database. Members of Congress themselves would give up a lucrative personal privilege — their holdings would have to go into diversified funds or blind trusts — and the officials covered by the bill are the ones who bear its cost.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Ordinary citizens watching for conflicts of interest

how_it_helps.text: It bars individual purchases and sales of stocks, commodities, futures, and cryptocurrency by members of Congress, the President and Vice President, Supreme Court Justices, Federal Reserve governors, and Fed bank presidents, allowing only diversified funds such as mutual funds and Treasury securities.

It requires officials entering office to divest conflicting holdings within 180 days or place them in a qualified blind trust, and imposes a civil penalty of at least 10% of the value of any trade made in violation.
It requires officials and their spouses and dependent children to report any federal loans, contracts, or grants they apply for or receive within 30-45 days, with a $500 fine for failure to report.

It extends financial disclosure and trading rules to federal judges and senior Federal Reserve bank officials, and adds a $500 fine for any official who fails to file a required stock transaction report.

It requires that all these disclosures be posted online in searchable, sortable, downloadable formats with public data access, making officials' finances easier for journalists and citizens to examine.

analysis.who_pays: The officials covered by the bill: members of Congress, the President and Vice President, Supreme Court Justices, Federal Reserve governors, Fed bank presidents, and federal judges, who would have to divest individual holdings, accept a ban on future trades, and file more disclosures with fines for missing them. No taxpayer money is spent.
analysis.who_pays_short: Members of Congress and senior federal officials

drawbacks.text: The bill covers only a small set of officials — Members of Congress, the President and Vice President, Supreme Court Justices, Federal Reserve governors, and Fed bank presidents — leaving out congressional staff and most executive branch officials who also see market-moving information.

Enforcement depends heavily on the ethics agencies: the $500 fine for missing a transaction report and the civil penalty for trading violations are set and administered by the same supervising ethics offices, and critics of similar proposals have argued fines this size are too small to deter well-off officials.

The ban applies to future conduct with a 180-day divestiture window, so sitting officials could sell holdings gradually, and securities held before taking office can be kept as long as they are not traded — meaning pre-existing concentrated portfolios could persist.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is a meaningful rule against a real conflict of interest: officials who write laws and set monetary policy would no longer be able to trade the stocks and cryptocurrencies those decisions move. The costs are real but modest — officials would have to shift to blind trusts or broad index funds, and the 180-day divestiture window plus the late effective dates give covered officials a long runway. The main design weakness is that most anti-abuse teeth rest on the ethics offices' own regulations and a $500 late-filing fine, which is small relative to typical congressional portfolios. On balance the bill targets a clear conflict problem with a mechanism (a trading ban plus forced divestiture) rather than more paperwork alone.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to three House committees when introduced, then to a subcommittee eight months later, and no committee ever voted on it before the Congress ended, so it never reached the House floor.

narrative.text: Representative Katie Porter introduced the bill on February 9, 2022, and it was referred to the Oversight and Reform, House Administration, and Judiciary Committees.
It attracted only 3 cosponsors, all Democrats.
On November 1, 2022, it was referred to the Judiciary Subcommittee on Courts, Intellectual Property, and the Internet — its last action of record.
No committee reported the bill and no chamber voted on it before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023, so the bill died.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Members of Congress and other senior officials who trade individual stocks keep that ability, and their federal payments stay off any expanded public disclosure database.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Stock-trading members of Congress and Fed officials

for.name: Rep. Katie Porter
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill banning stock trading by senior officials and expanding financial disclosure

against.name: House Oversight and Reform Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a markup or vote, leaving it in committee until the Congress ended

against.name: House leadership of both parties
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the House floor; the bill's only actions after introduction were committee referrals, indicating no member of leadership moved it forward

sides.party_line_note: Only 3 House Democrats cosponsored and no Republican did, but the bill never received a vote, so the parties' positions were never tested on the record.

industries.industry: Incumbent federal officeholders (Members of Congress, the President and Vice President, Supreme Court Justices, Fed governors and bank presidents)
industries.note: The bill would take away their ability to trade individual stocks, crypto, and commodities while in office, force divestiture or blind trusts, and expose their federal payments in searchable public databases. Their interest in blocking it runs directly against the public's interest in officials without trading conflicts.

industries.industry: Federal judiciary and Federal Reserve banks (as institutions)
industries.note: Judges and senior Fed bank officials would for the first time be subject to the STOCK Act's disclosure and trading rules and to public online filing, ending their exemption from congressional ethics law.
